The Fed cut rates by 50 basis points in September 2024 because the Committee stated it "has gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent, and judges that the risks to achieving its employment and inflation goals are roughly in balance." 

Job gains had slowed and unemployment had moved up, while inflation made further progress toward the 2 percent objective.

On 2008-12-16 the Fed cut rates by 75 basis points, to 0% to 0.25%. The vote was 10-0. Key line: “Since the Committee's last meeting, labor market conditions have deteriorated, and the available data indicate that consumer spending, business investment, and industrial production have declined.”

In June 2022, the Fed raised the target range for the federal funds rate by 75 basis points (0.75 percentage point) to 1-1/2 to 1-3/4 percent. 

The statement noted: "Inflation remains elevated, reflecting supply and demand imbalances related to the pandemic, higher energy prices, and broader price pressures."

In March 2020, the Federal Reserve cut rates because "The coronavirus outbreak has harmed communities and disrupted economic activity in many countries, including the United States." The Fed stated that "The effects of the coronavirus will weigh on economic activity in the near term and pose risks to the economic outlook." 

To support the economy, the Fed lowered the target range for the federal funds rate to 0 to 1/4 percent. When interest rates drop, borrowing costs generally fall. While mortgages follow the 10-year Treasury rather than the federal funds rate, lower rates across the board reduce borrowing costs for loans and lower interest earned on savings.

On January 3, 2001, the Fed lowered its target for the federal funds rate by 50 basis points to 6 percent. 

The Fed stated: "The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to lower its target for the federal funds rate by 50 basis points to 6 percent." 

It added that: "These actions were taken in light of further weakening of sales and production, and in the context of lower consumer confidence, tight conditions in some segments of financial markets, and high energy prices sapping household and business purchasing power."

At the June 30, 2004 meeting, the FOMC raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 1.25 percent in a unanimous 12-0 vote. 

The Committee noted that "output is continuing to expand at a solid pace and labor market conditions have improved." It judged that inflation pressures were partly transitory and stated that "policy accommodation can be removed at a pace that is likely to be measured." 

Higher federal funds rates generally raise borrowing costs for credit cards and variable loans. Mortgages follow the 10-year Treasury yield rather than the fed funds rate.

In December 2015, the Fed raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points, moving the target range to 0.25% to 0.5%. The vote was unanimous. 

The Fed stated that "the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 1/4 to 1/2 percent" because of "considerable improvement in labor market conditions this year".

In July 2019, the Fed cut interest rates by 25 basis points to a range of 2.0% to 2.25%. 

The Fed stated it acted "In light of the implications of global developments for the economic outlook as well as muted inflation pressures," noting that inflation was "running below 2 percent."

In July 2023, the Fed raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to a target range of "5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent" with a unanimous 11-0 vote. The Fed noted that "Inflation remains elevated" and that it was "strongly committed to returning inflation to its 2 percent objective." 

While this raised borrowing costs for credit cards and variable loans, mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury rather than the fed funds rate.

At its September 16, 2026 meeting, the Fed voted 12-0 to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent. 

The FOMC stated: "The Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate." It added that "Inflation remains elevated" and that "Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal."

Rate hikes generally raise borrowing costs like credit cards, while savings yields may rise. Mortgages follow the 10-year Treasury yield rather than the federal funds rate directly. 

Educational forecast models are not financial advice.

In June 2006, the FOMC raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5-1/4 percent. The vote was unanimous at 10 to 0. 

The Fed stated: "Readings on core inflation have been elevated in recent months" and noted that high resource utilization and energy prices "have the potential to sustain inflation pressures."

In September 2007, the Fed cut its target interest rate by 50 basis points (0.50 percentage points) to 4.75 percent. 

The FOMC stated, "Today’s action is intended to help forestall some of the adverse effects on the broader economy that might otherwise arise from the disruptions in financial markets and to promote moderate growth over time."

In December 2025, the FOMC lowered the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to a target range of "3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent" by a 9-3 vote. 

The Fed noted that "downside risks to employment rose in recent months" while "inflation has moved up since earlier in the year and remains somewhat elevated." Three members dissented, with one preferring a larger cut and two preferring no change. 

Lowering the federal funds rate generally reduces borrowing costs for credit cards and home equity lines, while savings yields tend to drift lower. Mortgages follow the 10-year Treasury yield rather than the federal funds rate directly.

At its October 2026 meeting, the Federal Reserve voted 10 to 2 to "maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent". Two officials dissented, preferring a quarter-point rate increase. 

The Fed noted that "Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace" and "Inflation remains elevated." 

For households, savings yields and credit card rates should remain steady, while mortgages follow the 10-year Treasury yield rather than the federal funds rate.

At its August 9, 2011 meeting, the Fed decided "to keep the target range for the federal funds rate at 0 to 1/4 percent." 

The Committee stated that "economic conditions--including low rates of resource utilization and a subdued outlook for inflation over the medium run--are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels for the federal funds rate at least through mid-2013." 

The vote was 7 to 3, with Richard W. Fisher, Narayana Kocherlakota, and Charles I. Plosser voting against.

At the December 2025 FOMC meeting, three members dissented: Stephen I. Miran preferred a 1/2 percentage point rate cut, while Austan D. Goolsbee and Jeffrey R. Schmid preferred no change to the target range.

Four FOMC members dissented at the April 2026 meeting:

Stephen I. Miran dissented because he "preferred to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting".

Beth M. Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie K. Logan dissented because they "supported maintaining the target range for the federal funds rate but did not support inclusion of an easing bias in the statement at this time".
At the September 2019 meeting, three members voted against the decision: James Bullard, Esther L. George, and Eric S. Rosengren.
At the September 2016 meeting, three members dissented from the decision to hold interest rates steady: Esther L. George, Loretta J. Mester, and Eric Rosengren.

At the September 18, 2024 meeting, Michelle W. Bowman was the sole dissenter. She "preferred to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting" rather than the 1/2 percentage point cut approved by the other 11 voting members.

A 25 basis point rate rise increases the monthly payment on a $400,000 mortgage from $2,725.99 to $2,794.12, a difference of $68.13 per month (assuming a starting rate of 7.24%). 

Note that 30-year mortgages follow the 10-year Treasury, not the Fed's target rate directly.

When the Fed hikes interest rates, credit card rates typically rise by the same amount because credit card APRs are tied to the prime rate. 

For a $5,000 balance at an average rate of 21.19%, a 50 basis point hike would increase your monthly interest charges by about $2.08, raising your monthly cost from $88.29 to $90.38, adding $25.00 over the year.

If the Fed cuts rates by 25 basis points, credit card interest rates—which are tied to the prime rate—typically drop by the same amount. 

For a $10,000 credit card balance at the current average rate of 21.19%, a 25 basis point reduction would lower your rate to 20.94%. Your monthly interest charge would decrease by about $2.08, saving you roughly $25 over a year. 

*This is a general educational overview, not personal financial advice.*

If your 30-year mortgage rate rises 50 basis points from 7.24% to 7.74%, a $300,000 mortgage will cost $102.67 more per month, bringing the payment from $2,044.49 to $2,147.16. 

Mortgage rates generally follow the 10-year Treasury yield rather than the Federal Reserve's short-term policy rate directly.

The Fed sets this interest rate to help manage inflation and support maximum employment. When the federal funds rate stays on hold, it generally keeps borrowing costs stable for consumers and businesses, though mortgage rates tend to track the 10-year Treasury yield rather than the federal funds rate directly.
